Cleanse the Conscience
klenz the KON-shens
verb phrase (Hebrews 9:14)
From the Authorized Version of Hebrews 9:14, the blood of Christ that purges the conscience from dead works; the cleansing of the inner moral judgment by the once-for-all sacrifice.

Biblical Definition

To cleanse the conscience is the work of the blood of Christ that purges the believer's inner moral judgment from the guilt of sin and from dead works, that he may serve the living God with freedom and assurance. The writer to the Hebrews sets it against the old sacrifices, which could sanctify outwardly but never reach the conscience: “How much more shall the blood of Christ, who through the eternal Spirit offered himself without spot to God, purge your conscience from dead works to serve the living God?” The conscience—the inner witness that accuses or excuses—is defiled by sin and burdened with guilt, and no ceremony, penance, or human work can wash it clean; only the blood of Christ, applied by faith, sprinkles the heart from an evil conscience. So the believer is bidden to draw near with a true heart in full assurance of faith, having his heart sprinkled from an evil conscience; and the answer of a good conscience toward God is given by the resurrection of Jesus Christ. The dictionary marks the cleansing of the conscience as a chief benefit of the finished work and the ground of the believer's peace with God. It holds the doctrine against two errors. The first is the Roman system of penance and works, which seeks to relieve the guilty conscience by human satisfactions that can never reach it. The second is the modern therapeutic counterfeit, which would quiet the conscience not by cleansing guilt but by denying it—reframing sin as mere brokenness and silencing the accusing witness rather than washing it. The dictionary holds that the conscience is cleansed, not silenced: real guilt is really purged by real blood, that the believer may serve the living God with a heart at peace.

Webster 1828 Definition

The work of the blood of Christ that purges the inner moral judgment from guilt and dead works (Hebrews 9:14), giving full assurance to serve the living God; against Roman penance that cannot reach it and therapeutic counterfeits that deny guilt rather than cleanse it.

CLEANSE THE CONSCIENCE, verb phrase. The purging of the inner moral judgment by the blood of Christ.

“The blood of Christ… purge your conscience from dead works to serve the living God” (Hebrews 9:14).

The old sacrifices could not reach the conscience; the blood of Christ does.

Draw near with hearts sprinkled from an evil conscience (Hebrews 10:22).

The conscience is cleansed of real guilt, not merely silenced.

Key Scripture

Heb 9:14 — "How much more shall the blood of Christ, who through the eternal Spirit offered himself without spot to God, purge your conscience from dead works to serve the living God?"

Heb 10:22 — "Let us draw near with a true heart in full assurance of faith, having our hearts sprinkled from an evil conscience, and our bodies washed with pure water."

1 Pe 3:21 — "The like figure whereunto even baptism doth also now save us (not the putting away of the filth of the flesh, but the answer of a good conscience toward God,) by the resurrection of Jesus Christ:"

1 Ti 1:5 — "Now the end of the commandment is charity out of a pure heart, and of a good conscience, and of faith unfeigned:"

Modern Corruption

Roman penance seeks to relieve the guilty conscience by works that cannot reach it; the therapeutic counterfeit quiets the conscience by denying guilt rather than cleansing it.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the conscience is cleansed of real guilt by real blood. The first corruption is the Roman system of penance and human satisfactions, which seeks to relieve the burdened conscience by works, indulgences, and ceremonies that, like the old sacrifices, can never reach it. The writer to the Hebrews is emphatic: the blood of bulls and goats could sanctify outwardly but not purge the conscience; only the blood of Christ does. To send the guilty soul to its own works for relief is to leave the conscience uncleansed.

The opposite and more modern corruption is the therapeutic counterfeit, which would quiet the conscience not by cleansing guilt but by denying it—relabelling sin as brokenness or woundedness, and silencing the accusing witness rather than washing it. But a conscience merely silenced is not a conscience cleansed; the guilt remains though the alarm is muted. The dictionary holds the gospel cure: the conscience is purged, not numbed. Real guilt is really removed by the blood of Christ applied by faith, so that the believer draws near in full assurance, his heart sprinkled from an evil conscience, free at last to serve the living God with a peace the world's techniques can never give.

Hebrew Roots

From “conscience” (Latin conscientia, joint-knowledge) and the Greek katharizo (to purge, cleanse); the inner moral witness purged from dead works by the blood of Christ.

expand to see more

Syneidesis, Greek, conscience, the inner witness that accuses or excuses.

Katharizo, Greek, to cleanse or purge, of the conscience purged by Christ's blood.

“Dead works,” the works of a guilty, unregenerate heart, from which it is cleansed.

Set against the old sacrifices, which could not reach the conscience.

The “answer of a good conscience” secured by the resurrection (1 Peter 3:21).

Usage

"The pastor preached the cleansed conscience to the guilt-burdened soul, pointing to the blood of Christ."

"He answered Roman penance: no human work can reach the conscience that Christ's blood purges."

"She found peace not by silencing guilt but by having it cleansed, drawing near in full assurance."
